tldr: WebDancer presents a data-centric, four-stage paradigm (browsing data construction, trajectory sampling, SFT, and RL via DAPO) for building autonomous multi-step information-seeking web agents based on the ReAct framework.
contributions: Two novel dataset synthesis pipelines: CRAWLQA (crawling authoritative websites and generating deep queries via GPT-4o) and E2HQA (iteratively evolving simple QA pairs into complex multi-step ones)
A four-stage training paradigm combining rejection sampling fine-tuning (Short-CoT and Long-CoT trajectories) followed by on-policy RL with the DAPO algorithm
WebDancer, instantiated on ReAct with search and click tools, achieving strong performance on GAIA and WebWalkerQA benchmarks
methods: The authors construct two synthetic datasets—CRAWLQA (crawling root URLs from sites like arxiv, github, wiki and using GPT-4o to generate QA pairs from subpages) and E2HQA (iteratively replacing entities with sub-questions to scale complexity). High-quality ReAct trajectories are sampled via rejection sampling using GPT-4o (Short-CoT) and QwQ-Plus (Long-CoT), then filtered through three stages: validity control, correctness verification, and quality assessment (limiting to ≤2 actions, checking non-redundancy, goal alignment, and logical accuracy). The model is first cold-start trained via SFT (masking observation tokens from loss), then refined with DAPO-based on-policy RL, which uses dynamic sampling to over-sample underutilized QA pairs and filter out prompts with perfect or zero accuracy.
results: WebDancer achieves a Pass@3 score of 64.1% on GAIA and 62.0% on WebWalkerQA. It substantially outperforms vanilla ReAct baselines across model scales and surpasses GPT-4o in the best-case scenario. RL yields substantial Pass@3 and Cons@3 improvements for non-reasoning models, with Post-RL Pass@1 comparable to SFT baseline Pass@3. For LRM-based agents, RL improvements in Pass@1, Pass@3, and Cons@3 are marginal, though consistency improves slightly.
limitations: RL improvements for LRMs are marginal, attributed to sparse reward signals from excessively long trajectories
Synthetically generated QA data may contain invalid or noisy instances that could degrade policy learning
Trajectory filtering restricts actions to ≤2, potentially discarding valid but longer reasoning paths
Test sets of existing benchmarks are small (GAIA: 466, WebWalkerQA: 680, BrowseComp: 1,266), limiting robust evaluation
